full_judgment: 4. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that the petitioner has been possessing the suit plot which is an undivided house for more that 30 years and he is entitled to buy the same under section 4 of the Partition Act and the learned Additional District Judge erred in law in deciding the case under section 4 of the Partition Act and as a result justice is denied to the petitioner. He further submitted that though the suit land is stated to be a chala land but it is a part and parcel of the petitioner's house where he grows vegetables and, as such, the suit land cannot be considered as a separate land from the dwelling house ?f the petitioner. In support of his above contention he relied on the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 53; 40 DLR(AD) 150, 10 DLR 318, 12 DLR 649; 20 DLR 489, 22 CWN. 575, AIR 1960 (Cal) 467, ILR (Cal) 873, IC 1940, 117 and 12 CU 525. In the case reported in 40 DLR (AD) 150 wherein their Lordships made an observation, after discussing the case laws reported in the aforesaid 22 CWN, AIR 1960 (Cal), 12 CU and some other similar cases of Indian High Courts. Similarly, the observation made by their Lordships in 12 DLR and 20 DLR as stated above is almost same. I shall discuss the above observations later on. In reply to the above submission Mr. Reazul Karim, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, submitted that the petitioner filed the pre-emption case and he lost and, as such, he is debarred from purchasing the suit land under section 4 of the Partition Act. He further submitted that opposite party possessed the suit land after purchasing the same and he was subsequently dispossessed from the suit land which made him to file the suit. He also submitted that the petitioner did not disclose how the suit land belonged to undivided family of the petitioner as the land was transferred as chala land and not as homestead and, as such, section 4 of the Partition Act is not applicable in this case. In support of the above contention he cited a decision reported in 36 DLR 350. It is admitted that one co-sharer ie defendant No.1, transferred his share in favour of his wife Safatunnessa on 22-7-42 and Safatunnessa possessed the same for more than 11 years and transferred the same to the opposite party No.1 by registered Kabala dated 22-11-1953. The defendant No.1 of the original suit filed a pre-emption case against the said transferor but the same was dismissed as barred by limitation. In the petition suit under section 4 of the Partition Act the defendant No.1 stated that the suit property is an undivided homestead and the suit land is the land of his purchased plot by 4 brothers including the defendant No.1 The court below held the view that the entire suit plot is not the undivided dwelling house of the defendant No.1 as the suit land has been described in khatian as chala land where vegetables are grown. Since the suit land is a part and parcel of land where other 3 brothers have got dwelling house, it is an adjacent land and part of the suit plot. It is admitted that the plaintiff-opposite party is a stranger purchaser. In a case reported in 40 DLR (AD) 150 (Sree Jugal Kishori Sarker vs. Azizur Rahman and others) their Lordships observed: "As to the meaning of dwelling house for the purpose of section 4 it was noticed: "The terms house or dwelling house are ambiguous terms and for the purpose of section 4 of the Partition Act must be liberally construed. The terms should be taken to mean not only the structure or building but also adjacent buildings, garden, courtyard, orchard, and all that is necessary for the convenient occupation of the house. In support of the proposition, we need refer to the following, from amongst numerous decisions on the point." Section 4 of the Partition Act was enacted for the benefit of the undivided members of the family against the stranger purchaser. Their Lordships Amin Ahmed CJ and Asir J in a case reported in 12 DLR 649 (Bhaba Kanta Joddar and others VS. Satish Chandra Mandai and others) observed: "The language of section 4 does not militate against the view that the object of the legislature being to prevent intrusion by strangers to the dwelling house of an undivided family, the terms of section 4 should be liberally construed." Similar view has been taken in a case repotted in 20 DLR 489 (Mohammad Habibullah and another VS. Moulvi Saleh Chowdhury and others) wherein their Lordships held: "Section 4 of the Partition Act was enacted to afford protection to the members of an undivided family against stranger purchaser Its simple object was to prevent intrusion into the dwelling house of an undivided family by strangers on the basis of purchase of some share in such dwelling house."
